```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(eval = FALSE, collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

Use `oauth_db_duckdb()` to query a remote DuckDB Quack server with each
visitor's OAuth access token. The connection works with DBI and dbplyr.
A local DuckDB file has no OAuth login; this helper connects to a server
that validates tokens and enforces its own data access policy.

## Prepare the server and client

Use compatible DuckDB and Quack versions on both sides. The R client needs
`duckdb` 1.5.3 or later and its matching `quack` and `httpfs` extensions. Quack's interface
has changed between releases, so test your chosen versions together.

```{r install}
install.packages("duckdb")
connection <- DBI::dbConnect(duckdb::duckdb(), dbdir = ":memory:")
DBI::dbExecute(connection, "INSTALL quack")
DBI::dbExecute(connection, "INSTALL httpfs")
DBI::dbDisconnect(connection, shutdown = TRUE)
```

Keep extensions in a directory the app can use across R sessions, for example
by setting `DUCKDB_EXTENSION_DIRECTORY` before provisioning and running the
app. The helper loads Quack inside a private in-memory DuckDB instance.

On the server, configure an OAuth validator such as
[quack_oauth](https://github.com/DataZooDE/quack-oauth). Follow that
extension's installation and server configuration instructions for your
DuckDB version and server platform. A client can connect even when
quack_oauth is unavailable for its own platform: only the server loads it.
Configure its trusted issuer and audience, select its
authentication and authorization callbacks, and define the scopes and
data access policy each visitor needs. Quack's default shared token check
does not validate OAuth tokens.

Expose the server through TLS with a certificate trusted by the DuckDB
client, typically through a reverse proxy. See
[Quack security](https://duckdb.org/docs/current/quack/security).
Pass `ca_bundle = "path/to/private-ca.pem"` if the server uses a private CA.
The helper explicitly enables TLS, including for loopback hosts.
For local development only, `allow_local_http = TRUE` permits HTTP on
`localhost`, `127.0.0.1` or `[::1]`.

`quack_oauth` also has client-side OAuth flows. They are unnecessary here:
shinyOAuth handles browser sign-in and renewal; the helper passes only the
resulting access token to Quack. It creates no persistent token secrets.

## Register the Shiny app

Register an OAuth client with the server's identity provider and allow
`http://localhost:8100` as a redirect URI. Request access tokens for the
audience configured on the Quack server. An ID token or a token issued for
another API cannot substitute for this access token.

This example uses an OIDC provider and the `quack:read` scope from
quack_oauth's default policy. Configure the provider to issue that scope
and the correct audience. Use your server's scopes if its policy differs.
Request `offline_access` too if your provider requires it for renewal.
For providers requiring a resource parameter or named token target, configure
that on the shinyOAuth client and pass the target name to `oauth_db_duckdb()`.

Save your registration in `.Renviron` and restart R:

```text
OAUTHDB_CLIENT_ID=your-client-id
OAUTHDB_CLIENT_SECRET=your-client-secret
OAUTHDB_DUCKDB_ISSUER=https://login.example.org/realms/reporting
```

## A complete app

Replace the hostname, port and table name for your deployment. This example
uses port 443 for a TLS proxy; Quack's default port is 9494.

```{r app}
library(shiny)
library(shinyOAuth)
library(shinyOAuthDB)

provider <- oauth_provider_oidc_discover(
  issuer = Sys.getenv("OAUTHDB_DUCKDB_ISSUER")
)
client <- oauth_client(
  provider,
  client_id = Sys.getenv("OAUTHDB_CLIENT_ID"),
  client_secret = Sys.getenv("OAUTHDB_CLIENT_SECRET"),
  redirect_uri = "http://localhost:8100",
  scopes = c("openid", "quack:read")
)

ui <- oauth_ui(fluidPage(
  actionButton("login", "Sign in"),
  actionButton("logout", "Sign out"),
  tableOutput("rows")
), id = "auth", client = client)

server <- function(input, output, session) {
  auth <- oauth_module_server("auth", client, auto_redirect = FALSE)
  observeEvent(input$login, auth$request_login())
  observeEvent(input$logout, auth$logout())

  con <- oauth_db_duckdb(
    auth$connection, host = "duckdb.example.org", port = 443,
    required_scopes = "quack:read"
  )
  output$rows <- renderTable({
    connection <- con()
    DBI::dbGetQuery(connection, "SELECT * FROM orders LIMIT 20")
  })
}

shinyApp(ui, server, options = list(port = 8100), uiPattern = ".*")
```

Run `shiny::runApp(port = 8100)`. The app waits for sign-in before connecting
and clears the output on sign-out. Get a connection inside each render or
reactive expression before running queries.

For dbplyr, use `dplyr::tbl(con(), "orders")`. The helper attaches the remote
catalog as `oauth_remote` and selects its `main` schema. Pass `schema` to
select another remote schema. Table queries use the attached catalog;
standalone expressions such as `SELECT current_user` can run locally and
do not prove which remote principal the server authenticated.

## Connection lifetime

Call `con()` before each operation. Quack receives a token when attaching,
so the helper closes and replaces the connection when the access token
changes. This ends transactions and discards temporary client state on
the old connection. Keep a transaction within one synchronous operation
and get a new handle for the next operation.

Account changes, lost required permissions, sign-out and Shiny session end
close the connection and shut down its private DuckDB instance. A caller
retaining a raw handle must still obtain `con()` before each operation;
the server decides whether an existing remote session remains authorized.
The helper never retries SQL statements or replays a transaction.

Setup errors omit the token-bearing SQL statement. An attachment failure
can mean an unavailable endpoint, a rejected TLS certificate or token,
denied catalog access, or an unknown schema. Check server diagnostics and
confirm the issuer, audience and scopes match the app registration.

For several accounts and saved results, see
[Authentication and sessions](authorization.html).

## Test the integration locally

The source checkout includes a
[Docker fixture](https://github.com/lukakoning/shinyOAuthDB/tree/main/integration/duckdb-oauth)
with a real quack_oauth server, a JWKS issuer and a TLS proxy. It generates
its own signed test tokens and certificates. From the repository root, run
`Rscript --vanilla tools/check-duckdb-oauth.R` with Docker running and the
test dependencies installed. The checks cover DBI/dbplyr reads, rejected
writes, invalid tokens and TLS verification without production credentials.
